newsitem.title: UK: Rifkind rebuts case for UK decision now on EMU.
newsitem.headline: Rifkind rebuts case for UK decision now on EMU.

text.p: Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind warned "Euro-sceptic" Conservatives that to take a decision now on whether to join a single currency would damage Britain's national interest and turn off voters.

In his keynote speech to the ruling Conservatives' annual conference, Rifkind said Britain needed to remain part of talks on EMU to ensure the convergence criteria were not fudged in ways that would cause economic instability across Europe.
"It is my sober and considered judgement that British interests on these crucial matters would be seriously damaged if we take premature decisions," Rifkind said.

Prime Minister John Major is under pressure from Euro- sceptics opposed to closer European ties to steal a march on Labour and fight the election, due by May, on a platform explicitly opposed to Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

But Rifkind said Britain -- and the Conservatives -- had nothing to lose by deferring a decision, especially because Major has pledged to hold a referendum if the cabinet votes to recommend EMU membership.
"To force a decision now just to differentiate ourselves from Labour would be to put party before country and, I suggest, the country would not be impressed," he said.

"So I say to my friends and colleagues who are calling for instant decisions on such an historic mater -- be patient. Neither the national interest nor the party interest require us to ride roughshod over views deeply and sincerely held.
"If the issue was forced now it would be like standing on the edge of a cliff expecting to benefit if one takes a great leap forward!" Rifkind said.
The tenor of Rifkind's remarks was less Euro-sceptical than a widely reported speech he gave last month in Switzerland in which he warned that EMU could split the EU.
While stressing that Britain wanted Europe to grow into an outward-looking partnership of nations and not a bureaucratic superstate, he spoke of Europe as an opportunity not a threat.

"We are part of Europe. Europe's future will influence our future. We must not be anti-European. We cannot be anti- European... No one can ignore the facts of geography. Our fate is intertwind with theirs," the foreign secretary said.
